practices.title: Empty catch block swallows exceptions
practices.description: Catching an exception and doing nothing hides failures until they surface somewhere confusing much later, instead of at the point they actually happened.
practices.risk: Data corruption or a broken downstream call goes unnoticed; the bug report that eventually comes in points nowhere near the real cause.

practices.title: Catching generic Exception instead of a specific type
practices.description: Catching Exception or Throwable masks unrelated failures, including unchecked bugs like a NullPointerException, as if they were the expected failure mode.
practices.risk: A real bug (NPE, ClassCastException) gets silently absorbed by handling meant for an expected, recoverable failure like a missing file.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*(Exception|Throwable)\s+\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Losing the original exception cause when wrapping
practices.description: Wrapping an exception in a new one without passing the original as the cause discards the stack trace that shows what actually failed.
practices.risk: Production incident logs show only the wrapper's generic message; diagnosing the real failure requires reproducing it from scratch.
practices.detectionPattern: throw\s+new\s+\w+Exception\("[^"]*"\)\s*;

practices.title: Throwing a generic RuntimeException with a vague message
practices.description: A bare RuntimeException("Error") tells the caller and the operator nothing about what went wrong or how to react to it.
practices.risk: An on-call engineer paged at 3am sees only 'Error' in the stack trace and has to read the surrounding code to find out what actually failed.
practices.detectionPattern: throw\s+new\s+(RuntimeException|Exception)\("(Error|Failed|Something went wrong)"\)

practices.title: Catching NullPointerException or ClassCastException as control flow
practices.description: NullPointerException and ClassCastException almost always indicate a programming bug, not an expected condition to branch on.
practices.risk: The actual bug (why the reference was null) is hidden behind a catch block that treats the crash as normal, so it never gets fixed and can resurface with worse consequences elsewhere.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*(NullPointerException|ClassCastException)\s+\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Returning null instead of Optional or an empty collection
practices.description: A null return forces every caller to remember a null check or risk an NPE far from the source. An empty List/Optional makes the absent case impossible to forget.
practices.risk: A caller that forgets the null check throws an NPE in production, often several layers away from where null originated.
practices.detectionPattern: return\s+null\s*;

practices.title: Returning null instead of an empty array
practices.description: Effective Java Item 54: a null array return forces every caller to add a null check that's easy to forget, mirroring the same problem as a null collection return.
practices.risk: A caller that iterates the result without a null check throws an NPE; this is especially easy to miss because arrays look like they should never be null.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: array-returning method with a null branch instead of an empty array

practices.title: String compared with == instead of .equals()
practices.description: == compares object identity, not content. Two equal strings from different sources (e.g. one from a DB read) can be == false while .equals() correctly returns true.
practices.risk: A conditional silently takes the wrong branch whenever the string wasn't interned the same way, e.g. after deserialization or string concatenation.

practices.title: Overriding equals() without hashCode() (or vice versa)
practices.description: Effective Java Item 11: equal objects must have equal hashCodes. Overriding one without the other breaks that contract.
practices.risk: The object is silently lost in a HashMap/HashSet: put() and get() with an 'equal' key can disagree on whether the entry exists, because they land in different hash buckets.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class overrides equals() but not hashCode(), or vice versa

practices.title: Comparing floating-point numbers with ==
practices.description: Floating-point arithmetic is imprecise; two values that are mathematically equal can differ in their last bits after a computation.
practices.risk: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluates to false in Java, so a guard relying on exact float/double equality silently takes the wrong branch.
practices.detectionPattern: double\s+\w+.*==\s*\d+\.\d+

practices.title: == on boxed types relying on autoboxing cache
practices.description: Integer/Long caching only covers -128 to 127. Two boxed values in that range can be == true by accident, creating a false impression that == works for boxed comparison.
practices.risk: Code that 'works' in testing with small numbers (e.g. quantities 1-10) breaks in production once a real value like 1000 is compared, because it falls outside the cache range.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: == comparison between two Integer/Long-typed variables

practices.title: Closeable resource opened without try-with-resources
practices.description: A stream/connection opened without try-with-resources leaks a file handle or connection if the code between open and close throws.
practices.risk: Under load, leaked file handles or DB connections exhaust the pool and the whole service starts failing unrelated requests.
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+(FileInputStream|FileOutputStream|BufferedReader|FileReader)\([^)]*\)\s*;

practices.title: Relying on finalize() for cleanup
practices.description: finalize() is deprecated since Java 9, runs at an unpredictable time (or never), and was never a reliable cleanup mechanism.
practices.risk: A file handle or connection 'cleaned up' only in finalize() may stay open far longer than expected, or forever if the GC never collects the object, exhausting a limited resource pool.
practices.detectionPattern: protected\s+void\s+finalize\s*\(

practices.title: Not closing AutoCloseable streams returned by Files.lines()/Files.list()
practices.description: Files.lines() and Files.list() open an underlying file handle/directory stream that must be closed.
practices.risk: Unlike in-memory streams, these implement AutoCloseable and leak file descriptors if not used in a try-with-resources block.
practices.code:
Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path);
lines.forEach(System.out::println); // file handle never closed
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Files.lines()/Files.list()/Files.walk() results assigned to a variable and used outside a try-with-resources block.

practices.title: Mutable HashMap shared across threads without synchronization
practices.description: HashMap is not thread-safe. Concurrent reads/writes from multiple threads can corrupt its internal structure or return stale/incorrect data.
practices.risk: Under concurrent load this can infinite-loop a thread (classic HashMap resize bug) or silently drop/return wrong entries — both hard to reproduce outside production traffic.
practices.code: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new HashMap<>();
practices.solution: private final Map<String, Session> sessions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+HashMap<[^>]*>\(\)

practices.title: Swallowing InterruptedException without restoring interrupt status
practices.description: Catching InterruptedException and doing nothing (or just logging) clears the thread's interrupt flag, so code further up the call stack that checks for cancellation never finds out.
practices.risk: A thread pool shutdown or task cancellation silently fails to stop this thread's work, because the interrupt signal was absorbed and never propagated.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: catch (InterruptedException e) block that doesn't call Thread.currentThread().interrupt()

practices.title: Forgetting lock.unlock() in a finally block
practices.description: Unlike synchronized, an explicit Lock is not automatically released. If the code between lock() and unlock() throws, and unlock() isn't in a finally block, the lock is held forever.
practices.risk: One exception permanently deadlocks every other thread that needs the same lock, with no exception or log pointing at the actual cause.

practices.title: Calling run() instead of start() on a Thread
practices.description: run() executes the Runnable's code on the current thread, synchronously. It does not create or start a new thread — only start() does that.
practices.risk: Code that looks concurrent (spawns a Thread, calls a method on it) actually runs entirely sequentially on the calling thread; any expected parallelism silently never happens.
practices.code:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> doWork());
t.run();  // runs in the calling thread!

practices.title: Relying on Thread.stop(), Thread.suspend(), or Thread.resume()
practices.description: These methods are deprecated because they're inherently unsafe: stop() can release locks mid-update and leave shared objects in a corrupted, half-modified state.
practices.risk: A thread killed via stop() mid-write can leave a shared data structure permanently corrupted, with no exception raised to indicate anything went wrong.
practices.code:
thread.stop();
thread.suspend();
practices.solution:
thread.interrupt();
// or a higher-level construct: ExecutorService.shutdownNow(), Future.cancel()
practices.detectionPattern: \.(stop|suspend|resume)\(\)\s*;

practices.title: Iterating a Collections.synchronizedList() without external synchronization
practices.description: Collections.synchronizedXxx() wrappers make individual method calls thread-safe, but iteration is not atomic.
practices.risk: Iterating without synchronizing on the collection itself can still throw ConcurrentModificationException if another thread mutates it mid-iteration.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: for-each loops over a Collections.synchronizedXxx() collection with no surrounding synchronized(collection) block.

practices.title: Non-atomic get-check-put pattern on ConcurrentHashMap instead of computeIfAbsent()/merge()
practices.description: Checking containsKey()/get() and then calling put() as separate steps is not atomic.
practices.risk: Two threads can interleave between the check and the write, causing lost updates or duplicate initialization, even on a thread-safe map implementation.
practices.solution:
cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensiveCompute(k)); // atomic check-and-set
// Or cache.merge(key, value, (old, v) -> combine(old, v)) for combining updates
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: containsKey()/get() followed by a conditional put() on a ConcurrentHashMap (or any map shared across threads) instead of a single atomic compute-family call.

practices.title: String concatenation in a loop
practices.description: Each += on a String allocates a new String; over N iterations this is O(n^2). StringBuilder amortizes to O(n).
practices.risk: Fine in a unit test with 5 rows, then times out or spikes latency once a real dataset with thousands of rows hits it.

practices.title: Creating unnecessary objects in a hot path
practices.description: Effective Java Item 6: creating an equivalent object repeatedly (a fresh regex Pattern, a new wrapper) when an immutable/reusable one would do wastes allocation and GC pressure for no benefit.
practices.risk: A method compiling the same regex on every call, or called in a loop over thousands of rows, spends measurable CPU time on object creation instead of the actual work.

practices.title: Using exceptions for ordinary control flow
practices.description: Effective Java Item 69: exceptions are for exceptional conditions. Using them to control a normal loop is slower than a plain condition check and obscures intent.
practices.risk: Throwing and catching an exception on every iteration of a hot loop costs orders of magnitude more than a bounds check, and confuses readers about whether the 'exceptional' path is actually expected.
practices.detectionPattern: catch\s*\(\s*ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

practices.title: Busy-waiting with Thread.sleep() instead of proper synchronization
practices.description: Polling a condition in a sleep loop wastes CPU and reacts late (up to one sleep interval late) instead of responding the instant the condition becomes true.
practices.risk: Under load, many busy-waiting threads burn CPU that real work needs, and the artificial polling delay adds latency that a wait/notify or CompletableFuture wouldn't have.
practices.solution:
task.thenAccept(this::processResult);
// or: CountDownLatch / Object.wait()-notify() for the blocking case
practices.detectionPattern: while\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{\s*Thread\.sleep

practices.title: Using Vector/Hashtable/StringBuffer in single-threaded code
practices.description: These legacy classes synchronize every method call. In code that's never accessed from multiple threads, that's pure overhead with no benefit — ArrayList/HashMap/StringBuilder do the same job faster.
practices.risk: Every single-threaded call pays a lock acquisition/release cost for no reason; under profiling this shows up as unexplained synchronization overhead in a supposedly single-threaded path.
practices.code:
Vector<Order> orders = new Vector<>();
StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();
practices.solution:
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
practices.detectionPattern: \bnew\s+(Vector|Hashtable|StringBuffer)\b

practices.title: Overusing parallelStream() without understanding overhead or thread-safety
practices.description: parallelStream() shares a common fork-join pool across the whole application.
practices.risk: For small collections or I/O-bound/non-thread-safe operations it can be slower than sequential and introduces race conditions on shared mutable state.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: parallelStream() on small collections, on I/O-bound operations, or pipelines that mutate shared non-thread-safe state.

practices.title: Using Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long> instead of IntStream/LongStream/DoubleStream for numeric work
practices.description: Stream<Integer> boxes every element, causing unnecessary object allocation and unboxing overhead during numeric aggregation compared to the dedicated primitive stream types.
practices.risk: A hot numeric aggregation path pays for boxing every element instead of running as fast, allocation-free primitive arithmetic.
practices.code:
Stream<Integer> nums = list.stream().map(Item::getQuantity);
int total = nums.reduce(0, Integer::sum); // boxes every element
practices.solution:
int total = list.stream()
    .mapToInt(Item::getQuantity)
    .sum(); // IntStream avoids boxing entirely
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Stream<Integer>/Stream<Long>/Stream<Double> pipelines used purely for sum/average/min/max instead of mapToInt/mapToLong/mapToDouble.

practices.title: Not setting initial capacity for collections with a known size
practices.description: Default collection capacities force repeated internal resizing and array copying as elements are added.
practices.risk: When the final size is known or estimable in advance, this is wasted work.
practices.code:
List<String> results = new ArrayList<>(); // default capacity 10
for (Row row : hugeResultSet) { // e.g. 100,000 rows
    results.add(row.toString()); // repeated resizes/copies as it grows
}
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: new ArrayList<>()/new HashMap<>() with no capacity argument, immediately followed by a loop with a known or easily obtainable bound.

practices.title: Using nested loops for lookups instead of building a Map for O(1) access
practices.description: Searching one list inside a loop over another produces O(n*m) complexity.
practices.risk: Indexing the smaller collection into a Map up front turns repeated lookups into O(1) each.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Nested loops where the inner loop searches for a matching element by field comparison instead of using a pre-built Map/Set.

practices.title: Using HashMap<EnumType, V> instead of EnumMap for enum-keyed maps
practices.description: EnumMap is implemented as a compact array indexed by enum ordinal, giving better performance and predictable (natural enum) iteration order compared to a general-purpose HashMap keyed by enum constants.
practices.risk: A map keyed by a small enum runs slower and iterates in an arbitrary order instead of the enum's natural declaration order, for no benefit over EnumMap.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: HashMap/TreeMap declared with an enum type as the key type parameter.

practices.title: Using findFirst() on a parallel stream when order doesn't matter
practices.description: findFirst() must respect encounter order even on a parallel stream, which forces extra coordination overhead.
practices.risk: When any matching element is acceptable, findAny() lets the runtime return as soon as one is found, which is faster in parallel.
practices.code:
Optional<Order> match = orders.parallelStream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.URGENT)
    .findFirst(); // forces ordered coordination even though caller doesn't care which URGENT order it gets
practices.solution:
Optional<Order> match = orders.parallelStream()
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == Status.URGENT)
    .findAny(); // no ordering constraint, faster in parallel
// Use findFirst() only when a deterministic, encounter-order result is actually required
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: findFirst() used after parallelStream() where the surrounding code doesn't depend on which specific match is returned.

practices.title: Filtering a stream twice instead of using Collectors.partitioningBy()
practices.description: Splitting a collection into two groups by a boolean predicate is commonly done with two separate filter() passes over the same source, which traverses the data twice when a single partitioningBy() collector does it in one pass.
practices.risk: The source collection is traversed twice to build two lists that a single partitioningBy() pass would produce from one traversal.
practices.code:
List<Order> paid = orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid).collect(Collectors.toList());
List<Order> unpaid = orders.stream().filter(o -> !o.isPaid()).collect(Collectors.toList()); // two full traversals
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Two filter()...collect() pipelines over the same source collection where the predicates are logical negations of each other.

practices.title: Recomputing Collections.max()/min() or sorting inside a loop instead of precomputing once
practices.description: Calling max()/min()/sort() on the same (or growing) collection repeatedly inside a loop is O(n) or O(n log n) per iteration, turning an otherwise linear algorithm into quadratic or worse.
practices.risk: An O(n) or O(n log n) computation that could run once instead re-runs on every loop iteration, turning a linear algorithm quadratic or worse.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Collections.max()/min()/sort() or stream().sorted()/max()/min() called inside a loop body where the underlying collection doesn't change between iterations.

practices.title: Not reordering stream operations for efficiency (sorting/mapping before filtering)
practices.description: Placing an expensive operation like sorted() or a costly map() before filter() forces it to run on every element, even ones that will be discarded.
practices.risk: Filtering first reduces the working set before the expensive step runs.
practices.code:
list.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Item::getExpensiveKey)) // sorts everything first
    .filter(Item::isActive) // then throws most of it away
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
practices.solution:
list.stream()
    .filter(Item::isActive) // shrink the working set first
    .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Item::getExpensiveKey)) // sort only what remains
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Stream pipelines where sorted()/map() with an expensive function precedes a filter() that would have reduced the element count.

practices.title: Making two separate stream passes to compute two aggregates instead of Collectors.teeing()
practices.description: Computing two different aggregates (e.g. sum and count, or min and max) by streaming the source collection twice does double the traversal work.
practices.risk: Collectors.teeing() (Java 12+) computes both in a single pass and merges the results.
practices.code:
double total = orders.stream().mapToDouble(Order::getAmount).sum(); // pass 1
long count = orders.stream().count(); // pass 2 — same source traversed again
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Two or more independent terminal operations invoked on separately-created streams from the same source collection within the same method.

practices.title: Using HashSet<EnumType> instead of EnumSet for enum-based sets
practices.description: EnumSet is a bit-vector implementation specialized for enum types, giving much better performance and memory usage than a general-purpose HashSet, plus iteration in natural (declaration) order.
practices.risk: A small, fixed enum-backed set pays general-purpose HashSet overhead instead of EnumSet's compact bit-vector representation, with no corresponding benefit.
practices.solution: Set<DayOfWeek> weekend = EnumSet.of(DayOfWeek.SATURDAY, DayOfWeek.SUNDAY); // compact, fast, ordered
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: HashSet/TreeSet declared with an enum type parameter instead of EnumSet.

practices.title: Public mutable fields instead of encapsulation
practices.description: A public non-final field lets any caller put the object into an invalid state directly, bypassing whatever validation the class's methods would otherwise enforce.
practices.risk: Nothing stops order.status = null or an invalid value from being set directly, and the bug surfaces far from where the bad assignment happened.
practices.detectionPattern: public\s+(?!final)\w+\s+\w+;

practices.title: Returning a mutable internal array/collection directly from a getter
practices.description: Handing out a direct reference to an internal mutable field lets the caller modify it and corrupt the object's internal state from outside, without going through any of the class's own methods.
practices.risk: Code far away from the class silently changes its internal list (e.g. clears it), and the class has no way to detect or prevent that mutation.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: getter returns a direct reference to a mutable field instead of a copy/unmodifiable view

practices.title: Classes/members left more accessible than they need to be
practices.description: Effective Java Item 15: minimize the accessibility of every class and member. A public class or field that only needs package-private (or private) visibility becomes part of the API surface, whether that was intended or not.
practices.risk: A field or class that was never meant to be public gets used from outside its package by another team, and now can't be changed or removed without breaking them.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public class/field with no external caller outside its own package

practices.title: No defensive copy of a mutable constructor argument
practices.description: Effective Java Item 50: storing a reference to a caller-supplied mutable object (instead of copying it) means the caller can keep a reference and mutate the 'immutable' object's internals after construction.
practices.risk: An object advertised as immutable (e.g. a date range used as a cache key) changes value after being stored, silently corrupting whatever relied on it staying constant.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor stores a mutable-typed parameter (Date, array, List) without copying it

practices.title: Using raw types instead of generics
practices.description: A raw type (List instead of List<Order>) disables generic type checking entirely, deferring what should be a compile error to a runtime ClassCastException.
practices.risk: A wrong-typed element added anywhere in the codebase compiles cleanly and only fails, with a confusing ClassCastException, at the unrelated line that reads it back out.
practices.detectionPattern: \b(List|Map|Set|Collection)\s+\w+\s*=\s*new\s+\w+\(\)

practices.title: int constants instead of an enum
practices.description: Effective Java Item 34: the 'int enum pattern' has no type safety — any int compiles where a status is expected, valid or not.
practices.risk: orderStatus = 99 compiles fine even though 99 isn't a real status, and printing the value gives a meaningless number instead of a readable name.
practices.solution:
public enum OrderStatus { PENDING, SHIPPED }

OrderStatus status = OrderStatus.PENDING; // only valid values compile
practices.detectionPattern: public\s+static\s+final\s+int\s+\w*_[A-Z]+\s*=

practices.title: Comparator chains that throw NullPointerException on null fields
practices.description: Comparator.comparing(Foo::getField) throws NPE the moment getField() returns null during a sort, instead of handling nulls explicitly with nullsFirst/nullsLast.
practices.risk: A sort that worked fine in testing throws NullPointerException in production the first time a real record has that field unset.
practices.code: list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getMiddleName)); // NPE if any middleName is null
practices.solution:
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getMiddleName,
    Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder())));
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Comparator.comparing() on a field/getter that is nullable, without nullsFirst/nullsLast wrapping.

practices.title: Creating generic arrays via unsafe casts (new Object[] cast to T[])
practices.description: Java forbids new T[] directly due to type erasure.
practices.risk: Developers work around this with an unchecked cast from Object[], which compiles with a warning but can throw ClassCastException later when the array is accessed as its erased type.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") near a cast of Object[] (or Object) to a generic array type T[].

practices.title: Calling Optional.get() without checking isPresent()/isEmpty() first
practices.description: Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty Optional, defeating the purpose of using Optional to avoid unchecked null-handling failures — it just moves the same class of bug to a different exception type.
practices.risk: Optional.get() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty Optional, moving the exact unguarded-absence failure Optional was meant to prevent into a different exception type.
practices.code:
Optional<User> user = repository.findById(id);
String name = user.get().getName(); // NoSuchElementException if not found
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Optional.get() calls not immediately preceded by an isPresent()/isEmpty() guard, or not replaced with map/orElse/orElseThrow/orElseGet chains.

practices.title: Relying on unsafe array covariance, risking ArrayStoreException
practices.description: Java arrays are covariant (String[] is-a Object[]) but that check is enforced at runtime, not compile time.
practices.risk: Storing an incompatible element through a supertype array reference compiles cleanly but throws ArrayStoreException at runtime.
practices.code:
Object[] objects = new String[3]; // legal — array covariance
objects[0] = Integer.valueOf(42); // compiles, but throws ArrayStoreException at runtime
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: A supertype array reference (e.g. Object[]) assigned from a subtype array instance, later written to via that supertype reference.

practices.title: Writing unbounded generic methods that require unsafe internal casts instead of adding proper bounds
practices.description: A generic method that needs to compare or otherwise operate on its type parameter should declare a bound like <T extends Comparable<T>>.
practices.risk: Without it, the implementation resorts to unchecked casts or reflection to work around the missing capability.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Generic methods with an unchecked cast of the type parameter to an interface (Comparable, Serializable, etc.) that could instead be expressed as a type bound.

practices.title: Shadowing an outer class's type parameter with a nested class or method's own type parameter of the same name
practices.description: Reusing a type parameter name like T in a nested class or generic method inside an already-generic outer class silently shadows the outer T, so code that intends to reference the outer class's type parameter actually binds to the unrelated inner one, defeating type checking without any compiler error.
practices.risk: A method or nested class believed to operate on the enclosing class's type parameter is silently working with an unrelated, unconstrained one instead, and the compiler gives no warning.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: A generic method or nested class declaring a type parameter with the exact same name as an enclosing generic class's type parameter.

practices.title: Using raw generic types when interacting with legacy APIs instead of re-establishing type safety at the boundary
practices.description: Pre-generics legacy libraries or reflection-based code often return raw types (e.g. raw List, Map).
practices.risk: Passing that raw reference around unchanged propagates the loss of type safety through the rest of the codebase instead of validating and re-typing it once at the boundary.
practices.code:
List legacyResults = legacyApi.fetchData(); // raw type from an old library
processResults(legacyResults); // raw type propagates, no compiler help anywhere downstream
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Raw-typed variables (List, Map, Set with no generic parameter) originating from a legacy or reflection-based call, passed to more than one downstream method unchanged.

practices.title: Ignoring compiler warnings instead of fixing them
practices.description: An unchecked or deprecation warning is the compiler telling you it found something it couldn't fully verify. Suppressing or ignoring it routinely means real bugs get waved through along with the noise.
practices.risk: A genuine unchecked-cast bug sits next to dozens of routinely-ignored warnings, indistinguishable from the noise, until it fails at runtime.
practices.detectionPattern: @SuppressWarnings\("unchecked"\)

practices.title: Missing @Override on an intended override
practices.description: Without @Override, a typo'd method signature silently compiles as a brand new overload instead of failing to compile, and the intended override never runs.
practices.risk: A subclass 'overrides' equals(Object o) but actually writes equals(MyClass o) — an overload, not an override — and the superclass's equals() keeps running unnoticed.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: method named equals/hashCode/toString without an @Override annotation

practices.title: Overusing static state
practices.description: Static mutable fields are effectively global variables — shared across every caller, hard to isolate in tests, and a source of hidden coupling between unrelated code paths.
practices.risk: A test that mutates the static state leaks that change into the next test, causing flaky, order-dependent test failures that are hard to reproduce.
practices.detectionPattern: public\s+static\s+(?!final)\w+\s+\w+;

practices.title: instanceof/casting chains instead of polymorphism
practices.description: A growing if/else-if chain checking an object's runtime type and casting it is exactly what virtual dispatch (an overridden method) is meant to replace.
practices.risk: Every new subtype requires finding and updating every instanceof chain across the codebase; missing one is a silent bug, not a compile error.
practices.detectionPattern: instanceof\s+\w+.*else\s+if\s*\([^)]*instanceof

practices.title: Long methods / God classes doing too much
practices.description: A method or class handling several unrelated responsibilities (validation, persistence, notification, formatting) is impossible to test in isolation and risky to change — every edit risks breaking an unrelated concern.
practices.risk: A one-line fix to the notification logic requires understanding and re-testing the entire method, including the unrelated persistence and validation code that method also does.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: method body exceeding roughly 80-100 lines mixing multiple unrelated responsibilities

practices.title: Deep inheritance hierarchies instead of composition
practices.description: Favoring composition ("has-a") over inheritance ("is-a") when there's no true substitutability relationship keeps a change three levels up from rippling unpredictably through every subclass.
practices.risk: A behavior change in a base class two or three levels up breaks a subclass's assumptions in a way that's hard to trace back to the actual change.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: inheritance chain deeper than 2-3 levels for a non-framework class

practices.title: Hardcoding a dependency instead of injecting it
practices.description: Effective Java Item 5: a class that constructs its own collaborator internally can't be tested with a fake/mock and can't be reconfigured without editing the class's source.
practices.risk: Writing a unit test for this class requires the real dependency (a real DB connection, a real HTTP client) to exist and work, turning a unit test into a slow, flaky integration test.
practices.detectionPattern: private\s+final\s+\w+\s+\w+\s*=\s*new\s+\w+\(

practices.title: Inheritance used for code reuse across unrelated classes
practices.description: Effective Java Item 18: extending a class purely to reuse its methods (not because of a genuine is-a relationship) couples the subclass to the superclass's implementation details, which can change underneath it.
practices.risk: A superclass method the subclass never even calls changes its internal behavior in a library upgrade, and the subclass breaks in a way nobody expected because it was never really a semantic subtype.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class extends a concrete collection/utility class purely to add instrumentation

practices.title: A class designed for inheritance with no documentation of overridable behavior
practices.description: Effective Java Item 19: if a class permits subclassing, it must document exactly how its methods interact — or explicitly prohibit inheritance (final, or a private constructor).
practices.risk: A subclass overrides a method the base class secretly calls from its own constructor, and the override runs before the subclass's own fields are initialized, producing confusing null/zero values.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor calls an overridable (non-final, non-private) instance method

practices.title: Using an abstract class where an interface would give more flexibility
practices.description: Effective Java Item 20: a class can only extend one abstract class but can implement many interfaces. Choosing an abstract class as the contract forecloses a consumer's ability to also extend something else.
practices.risk: A class that needs to satisfy this contract and also extend an unrelated base class (e.g. a framework's base class) simply can't, because Java has no multiple inheritance of classes.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: abstract class with only abstract methods and no shared state/implementation

practices.title: Using clone() to copy an object
practices.description: Object.clone() has a famously broken contract (it doesn't call constructors, interacts badly with final fields, and Cloneable carries no visible clone() method). A copy constructor or static factory is simpler and safer.
practices.risk: A subclass added later inherits a clone() that shallow-copies fields it doesn't know about, or throws CloneNotSupportedException in a place nobody expected an exception.
practices.detectionPattern: @Override\s*\n\s*public\s+\w+\s+clone\s*\(

practices.title: Using reflection without strong justification
practices.description: Reflection bypasses normal access control and type checking, is brittle across refactors (a renamed field breaks it silently until runtime), and is significantly slower than a direct call.
practices.risk: A routine rename of a private field compiles cleanly everywhere except the reflective access, which now throws NoSuchFieldException only when that code path actually runs.
practices.detectionPattern: \.getDeclaredField\(|\.setAccessible\(true\)

practices.title: Calling System.exit() from library or business logic
practices.description: System.exit() terminates the entire JVM immediately — not just the current request or operation. In a server, container, or test runner, that takes down every other in-flight request with it.
practices.risk: A single invalid-config check in a rarely-used code path kills the whole running application (or test suite) instead of just failing the one operation that hit it.
practices.detectionPattern: System\.exit\(

practices.title: Relying on the order of static initialization blocks
practices.description: Static field/block initialization order depends on declaration order within the class and load order across classes — easy to get subtly wrong and hard to see just by reading one class.
practices.risk: Reordering two unrelated-looking static declarations (or splitting a class into two files) silently changes which value a static field ends up with, with no compiler warning.
practices.solution:
// Keep static initialization simple and independent, or use lazy/explicit
// initialization instead of interdependent static blocks.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple interdependent static initializer blocks in one class

practices.title: Using assert for runtime validation in production code
practices.description: Java assertions are disabled by default (the JVM needs -ea to enable them), so an assert used for business validation silently does nothing in a standard production deployment.
practices.risk: A precondition check written as `assert amount > 0` never actually runs in production, so invalid data sails straight through into logic that assumed it was checked.

practices.title: Value objects that should be immutable but aren't
practices.description: Effective Java Item 17: a value-like object (Money, DateRange, Point) with setters can be mutated by any holder, and that mutation is invisible to every other piece of code holding the same reference.
practices.risk: A Money object passed into a pricing calculation gets mutated by that calculation, and the caller's own copy silently changes value even though they never called a setter themselves.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: class with a setter for a field that conceptually represents a fixed value (money, date range, coordinate)

practices.title: Modifying a collection while iterating it with a for-each loop
practices.description: Calling list.remove()/add() on the collection itself during a for-each loop (rather than via the Iterator) throws a ConcurrentModificationException — even single-threaded.
practices.risk: Removing an item conditionally inside a for-each loop throws at runtime the moment more than one item needs removing, a bug that's easy to miss in a quick manual test with only one matching item.
practices.solution: orders.removeIf(Order::isCancelled);

practices.title: Mutating an object after it's used as a Set element or Map key
practices.description: HashSet/HashMap place an element by its hashCode() at insertion time. Changing a field that hashCode() depends on afterward moves the object logically, but not physically — it's now in the wrong bucket.
practices.risk: contains()/get() on the exact same object reference returns false/null after the mutation, because the hash-based lookup checks the new (changed) bucket while the entry still lives in the old one.
practices.solution:
// Prefer immutable objects (or records) as Set elements / Map keys,
// so there's no setter that could invalidate the hash after insertion.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: an object added to a HashSet/HashMap has a setter called on it afterward

practices.title: Mutating a list returned by Arrays.asList()
practices.description: Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list backed by the array.
practices.risk: Calling add(), remove(), or clear() throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime, not compile time.
practices.code:
List<String> names = Arrays.asList("a", "b", "c");
names.add("d"); // throws UnsupportedOperationException
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Result of Arrays.asList(...) passed around and later mutated, especially several calls away from where it was created.

practices.title: Mutating immutable collections from List.of()/Map.of()/Set.of()
practices.description: Factory methods List.of(), Map.of(), and Set.of() (Java 9+) return truly immutable collections.
practices.risk: Any mutation attempt throws UnsupportedOperationException, unlike Collections.unmodifiableList wrapping a still-mutable backing list.
practices.code:
List<String> items = List.of("a", "b");
items.set(0, "z"); // throws UnsupportedOperationException
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Calls to .of() factory methods whose result is later passed to code that adds/removes/sets elements.

practices.title: Using HashMap when insertion or access order matters
practices.description: HashMap makes no guarantee about iteration order, which can change across JVM versions or even between runs.
practices.risk: Code that implicitly depends on insertion or sorted order will behave inconsistently.
practices.solution:
Map<String, Integer> scores = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // preserves insertion order
// or: new TreeMap<>() when sorted-key order is required
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: HashMap used where output/iteration order is visible to the user or asserted on in tests, without an explicit ordering requirement being met.

practices.title: Relying on List/Set.contains() for custom objects without overriding equals()/hashCode()
practices.description: contains(), indexOf(), and remove() on collections use equals() (and hashCode() for hash-based collections) to find a match.
practices.risk: Without a correct override, lookups silently fail even though an 'equal' element is logically present.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Custom classes stored in List/Set/Map and later looked up with contains()/indexOf()/remove() that don't override equals()/hashCode().

practices.title: Calling Collections.sort() directly on a list obtained from an unmodifiable/immutable source
practices.description: Collections.sort() sorts in place.
practices.risk: Calling it on a list backed by an unmodifiable wrapper or an immutable factory result (List.of(), Collections.unmodifiableList()) throws UnsupportedOperationException.
practices.code:
List<String> names = Collections.unmodifiableList(source);
Collections.sort(names); // throws UnsupportedOperationException
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Collections.sort()/list.sort() called on a variable assigned from List.of(), Collections.unmodifiableList(), or a method known to return an immutable view.

practices.title: Ambiguity between List.remove(int index) and List.remove(Object) with boxed Integer
practices.description: List<Integer> has two overloads: remove(int index) removes by position, remove(Object o) removes by value.
practices.risk: Passing a primitive int silently calls the index overload even when the intent was to remove a value, deleting the wrong element.
practices.code:
List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 30));
nums.remove(20); // removes element at INDEX 20 -> IndexOutOfBoundsException, or worse, removes wrong index if list is large
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: list.remove(intLiteralOrVariable) calls on a List<Integer>/List<Long> where the intent (by reading context) is to remove a value, not a position.

practices.title: Assuming Collections.unmodifiableList() provides deep immutability
practices.description: Collections.unmodifiableList() (and List.of()) only prevents structural changes to the list itself (add/remove/set).
practices.risk: The elements inside remain fully mutable if their own class exposes setters, so 'read-only' callers can still corrupt shared state.
practices.code:
List<Order> readOnly = Collections.unmodifiableList(orders);
readOnly.get(0).setStatus("CANCELLED"); // compiles fine, mutates the shared Order object
practices.solution:
List<Order> readOnly = orders.stream()
    .map(Order::copy) // defensive copy, or use an immutable record/value type
    .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList());
readOnly.get(0).setStatus("CANCELLED"); // compile error if Order is immutable
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Collections.unmodifiableList()/List.of() results whose element type is mutable (has public setters) and is passed to untrusted or external code.

practices.title: Using a Comparator in TreeMap/TreeSet that is inconsistent with equals()
practices.description: TreeMap/TreeSet use their Comparator (not equals()) to decide whether two elements are 'the same'.
practices.risk: If the comparator considers two logically distinct objects equal (returns 0), one silently overwrites or excludes the other.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: TreeMap/TreeSet constructed with a Comparator that only compares a subset of fields that don't uniquely identify distinct objects.

practices.title: Calling Iterator.next() without a matching hasNext() check
practices.description: Manually driving an Iterator by calling next() more times than there are elements throws NoSuchElementException.
practices.risk: This is easy to introduce when refactoring a for-each loop into a manual while loop incorrectly.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Manual Iterator.next() calls inside a loop whose condition doesn't call hasNext() on the same iterator.

practices.title: Assuming PriorityQueue's iterator returns elements in priority order
practices.description: PriorityQueue only guarantees that peek()/poll() return the smallest (or highest-priority) element.
practices.risk: Its iterator() traverses the internal heap array in an unspecified order, not sorted order.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: for-each or iterator() usage on a PriorityQueue where the code expects sorted output, instead of repeated poll()/peek().

practices.title: Treating ArrayList.subList() as an independent copy instead of a live view
practices.description: subList() returns a view backed by the original list.
practices.risk: Structural changes to either the sublist or the original list (other than through the sublist itself) throw ConcurrentModificationException on subsequent access.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: subList() result stored in a variable and used after further structural modifications to the original list, without wrapping subList() in new ArrayList<>().

practices.title: Implementing an LRU cache with LinkedHashMap but forgetting accessOrder=true
practices.description: LinkedHashMap defaults to insertion order.
practices.risk: An LRU cache needs access order so that reads (get()) move an entry to the most-recently-used position — without the accessOrder constructor flag and a removeEldestEntry() override, eviction logic silently removes the wrong entries.
practices.code:
Map<String, Object> cache = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, false); // insertion order — wrong for LRU
// eviction based on this order removes the oldest-inserted entry, not the least-recently-used one
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: LinkedHashMap constructed for caching purposes without the three-argument constructor and accessOrder=true, or without overriding removeEldestEntry().

practices.title: Inserting null elements/keys into TreeSet, TreeMap, or ConcurrentHashMap
practices.description: TreeSet/TreeMap need to compare elements to place them, so a null throws NullPointerException immediately on insertion.
practices.risk: ConcurrentHashMap explicitly disallows null keys and values to avoid ambiguity between 'absent' and 'mapped to null'. Code written against HashMap (which permits nulls) breaks when swapped to these types.
practices.code:
Map<String, String> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
map.put("key", null); // throws NullPointerException — silently worked with HashMap
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Code migrating from HashMap/HashSet to TreeMap/TreeSet/ConcurrentHashMap/ConcurrentSkipListMap without auditing for possible null keys or values.

practices.title: Filling a collection of collections with the same mutable reference (e.g. Collections.nCopies or a reused row)
practices.description: Collections.nCopies() and naive loop patterns that reuse one mutable object reference across multiple slots make every slot point to the same object.
practices.risk: Mutating one 'copy' mutates all of them, since no independent instances were ever created.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Collections.nCopies() (or a loop that adds the same variable reference repeatedly) used to build a collection of mutable objects, especially nested lists/arrays.

practices.title: Assuming ArrayList.clone() performs a deep copy
practices.description: List/Collection clone() methods (where available) perform a shallow copy — a new list is created, but the elements themselves are the same references as in the original, so mutating a shared element affects both lists.
practices.risk: Mutating an element through the supposedly independent cloned list silently mutates the same shared object still referenced by the original list.
practices.code:
ArrayList<Order> copy = (ArrayList<Order>) original.clone();
copy.get(0).setStatus("CANCELLED"); // mutates the SAME Order object referenced by 'original'
practices.solution:
List<Order> copy = original.stream()
    .map(Order::copy) // explicit deep-copy method on Order
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
copy.get(0).setStatus("CANCELLED"); // original is unaffected
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: .clone() called on a List/Collection of mutable elements, followed by mutation of an element through the cloned reference.

practices.title: Calling Iterator.remove() before calling next()
practices.description: Iterator.remove() removes the element most recently returned by next().
practices.risk: Calling it before next() has been invoked at all (or twice in a row without an intervening next()) throws IllegalStateException.
practices.code:
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
it.remove(); // IllegalStateException — next() was never called
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Iterator.remove() calls not immediately preceded (in the same loop iteration) by exactly one next() call on the same iterator.

practices.title: Using a List where uniqueness is a business requirement, allowing silent duplicate entries
practices.description: When the domain rule is 'no duplicates', storing elements in a List relies on every call site remembering to check for duplicates manually.
practices.risk: A Set enforces the invariant structurally so a duplicate simply can't be added.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: List fields/variables whose business meaning implies uniqueness (e.g. 'subscribers', 'tags', 'ids') with no duplicate-checking logic at the point of insertion.

practices.title: Using toArray(new T[size]) with a stale or incorrect size instead of toArray(new T[0])
practices.description: Passing a pre-sized array to toArray() that doesn't match the collection's current size either gets padded with a trailing null (if too large) or forces a fresh internal allocation anyway (if too small).
practices.risk: ToArray(new T[0]) always lets the JVM allocate exactly the right size and is the recommended idiom.
practices.code: String[] arr = list.toArray(new String[10]); // if list has 7 elements, arr[7..9] are null; if list grew since 10 was chosen, silently wrong
practices.solution: String[] arr = list.toArray(new String[0]); // always correctly sized, and JIT-optimized to be as fast as a pre-sized array
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: toArray(new T[N]) calls where N is a hardcoded or previously-cached size rather than 0 or list.size().

practices.title: Calling map.remove()/put() inside forEach() over the same map
practices.description: Map.forEach() (like other internal iteration methods) does not tolerate structural modification of the map during traversal.
practices.risk: Adding or removing entries from within the lambda throws ConcurrentModificationException just as it would in a for-each loop.
practices.solution:
map.entrySet().removeIf(entry -> entry.getValue().isExpired()); // safe, designed for in-place removal
// Or collect keys to remove first, then remove them in a separate pass
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: map.remove()/put()/clear() called on the same map instance from within its own forEach()/for-each iteration lambda.

practices.title: Assuming Collections.synchronizedMap() makes compound operations atomic
practices.description: synchronizedMap() only synchronizes individual method calls (get, put, etc.).
practices.risk: A sequence like get-check-put or size-then-modify is not atomic, so races between threads can still corrupt state even though every single call is thread-safe in isolation.
practices.solution:
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum); // single atomic compound operation
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Multiple sequential calls (get then put, containsKey then put, size then modify) on a Collections.synchronizedXxx() collection, treated as if the sequence itself were atomic.

practices.title: Recursing over deeply nested collections without a depth or stack-safety check
practices.description: Recursive traversal of arbitrarily deep nested structures (trees, nested lists/maps from JSON, category hierarchies) can exhaust the call stack with a StackOverflowError on unexpectedly deep or malicious input, where an iterative approach with an explicit stack would degrade gracefully.
practices.risk: Sufficiently deep or adversarial input (nested JSON, a crafted category tree) crashes the whole request with a StackOverflowError instead of failing gracefully.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Recursive methods traversing structures whose depth is determined by external/untrusted input (JSON, XML, user-defined hierarchies) with no depth limit.

practices.title: Mixing stack semantics (push/pop) and queue semantics (offer/poll) on the same Deque instance
practices.description: Deque supports both stack (push/pop/peek operate on the head) and queue (offer/poll operate on the tail-in/head-out) usage patterns.
practices.risk: Using both styles interchangeably on one instance produces confusing, order-dependent bugs because push() and offer() insert at opposite ends.
practices.code:
Deque<Task> tasks = new ArrayDeque<>();
tasks.push(taskA); // inserts at head
tasks.offer(taskB); // inserts at TAIL — inconsistent with push semantics
Task next = tasks.pop(); // removes from head — may not be the order the caller expects
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: The same Deque variable receiving both push()/pop() calls and offer()/poll() calls within the same class or method.

practices.title: Assuming List.copyOf() behaves exactly like Collections.unmodifiableList()
practices.description: List.copyOf() (Java 10+) creates a genuinely independent immutable copy and throws NullPointerException if any element is null.
practices.risk: Collections.unmodifiableList() merely wraps the original (still tolerating nulls and reflecting later changes to the source), so swapping between them without checking null-safety breaks previously-working code.
practices.solution:
List<String> copy = source.stream().anyMatch(Objects::isNull)
    ? Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(source)) // tolerate nulls if that's intentional
    : List.copyOf(source); // use when nulls are genuinely disallowed
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Migrations from Collections.unmodifiableList()/unmodifiableSet() to List.copyOf()/Set.copyOf() without auditing the source for possible null elements.

practices.title: Inconsistent Objects.requireNonNull() usage allowing partially-null domain objects into collections
practices.description: Validating some constructor parameters with requireNonNull() but not others lets objects with unexpected null fields slip into lists/maps, where the null surfaces much later (e.g.
practices.risk: during a sort, a hashCode computation, or a stream operation) far from its true origin, making the failure hard to trace.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Constructors validating some but not all reference-type parameters with requireNonNull(), especially on classes stored in collections.

practices.title: Continuing to mutate a builder after adding its built result to a collection
practices.description: If a builder's build() method returns a live reference to its internal mutable state rather than a defensive copy, reusing the same builder instance for the next entry retroactively corrupts every previously-built object already stored in the collection.
practices.risk: Reusing one builder instance across a loop retroactively corrupts every previously-built object already added to the collection, if build() doesn't defensively copy its state.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: A single builder instance reused across loop iterations where build() is documented (or observed) to return a mutable, non-copied result.

practices.title: Not documenting or enforcing the thread-safety of a returned collection
practices.description: A method that returns a collection without stating (in Javadoc or its type) whether it's safe for concurrent access forces every caller to guess.
practices.risk: Callers who assume thread-safety when there is none introduce silent race conditions, while callers who over-synchronize a genuinely safe collection add needless contention.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Public methods returning a collection field directly, with no Javadoc statement about thread-safety and no indication in the return type (e.g. an unqualified Collection/List/Map).

practices.title: Ambiguous method overloads with varargs/autoboxing
practices.description: Overloads that differ only by a boxed vs. primitive type, or that mix a fixed-arity overload with a varargs one, can resolve to a different method than the author intended, silently.
practices.risk: Adding a new overload later changes which existing overload a call site resolves to, without any compile error, because overload resolution rules are subtle and easy to get wrong.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: multiple overloads of the same method name differing only in boxed/primitive or varargs form

practices.title: Telescoping constructors for many optional parameters
practices.description: Effective Java Item 2: a chain of constructors adding one more optional parameter each time forces callers to pass values they don't care about just to reach the one they need, and it's easy to swap two same-typed arguments by mistake.
practices.risk: A caller passing (10, 5, true, false) to a 4-parameter constructor swaps the two booleans without any compile error, and the bug isn't visible until the wrong behavior shows up at runtime.
practices.solution:
Pizza pizza = Pizza.builder()
    .size(12)
    .cheese(true)
    .pepperoni(false)
    .build();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: chain of 3+ overloaded constructors each calling this(...) with one more parameter

practices.title: No Builder pattern for a class with many constructor parameters
practices.description: Effective Java Item 2: beyond roughly 4 constructor parameters (especially several of the same type), positional arguments become genuinely hard to get right at every call site.
practices.risk: Two adjacent String or int parameters get passed in the wrong order; it compiles fine and fails silently or produces subtly wrong behavior.
practices.code: new Order("user-123", "addr-1", "addr-2", true, false, 3, 19.99);
practices.solution:
Order.builder()
    .userId("user-123")
    .shippingAddress("addr-1")
    .billingAddress("addr-2")
    .giftWrap(true)
    .expedited(false)
    .quantity(3)
    .price(19.99)
    .build();
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: constructor call with 5+ positional arguments of primitive/String type

practices.title: The constant-interface antipattern
practices.description: Effective Java Item 22: an interface that exists only to declare constants leaks those constants into the public API of every class that implements it, whether or not that class wants them exposed.
practices.risk: Implementing the interface for its constants also commits every implementing class to exposing them publicly forever, and removing the constants later is a breaking change for classes that only ever wanted the behavior, not the constants.
practices.detectionPattern: interface\s+\w+\s*\{\s*(double|int|String)\s+[A-Z_]+\s*=

practices.title: Declaring a variable by its implementation type instead of its interface
practices.description: Effective Java Item 64: declaring HashMap<String, Order> instead of Map<String, Order> locks every line that uses it to the concrete implementation, even though nothing about the logic actually needs it.
practices.risk: Swapping HashMap for a LinkedHashMap or a concurrent variant later requires hunting down every declared-as-HashMap variable across the codebase instead of changing one line at the construction site.
practices.code: HashMap<String, Order> ordersByUserId = new HashMap<>();
practices.solution: Map<String, Order> ordersByUserId = new HashMap<>();
practices.detectionPattern: \b(HashMap|ArrayList|HashSet|LinkedList)<[^>]*>\s+\w+\s*=

practices.title: Inventing a custom exception where a standard one already fits
practices.description: Effective Java Item 72: IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, and similar standard types already cover most common error conditions. An ad hoc custom type for the same situation isn't recognized by tooling or reviewers the way the standard ones are.
practices.risk: A caller writing a catch block for the well-known IllegalArgumentException doesn't catch this class's homemade InvalidQuantityException, and the error propagates further than intended.
practices.detectionPattern: class\s+\w*Exception\s+extends\s+(RuntimeException|Exception)

practices.title: Ignoring the PECS principle (Producer-Extends, Consumer-Super) with bounded wildcards
practices.description: Using an unbounded or wrongly-bounded generic type where a wildcard is needed makes APIs unnecessarily rigid — callers can't pass a List<Integer> to a method expecting List<Number>, even though that should be safe for a read-only producer.
practices.risk: A caller holding a List<Integer> can't pass it to a method that should logically accept it for read-only use (one expecting List<Number>), forcing an unnecessary copy or a more permissive, less safe signature.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Generic method parameters typed as List<T>/Collection<T> that only read (producer) or only write (consumer) from the collection, without ? extends / ? super where flexibility is needed.

practices.title: Not using Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()/toUnmodifiableSet()/toUnmodifiableMap() when the result should never be mutated
practices.description: Collectors.toList()/toSet()/toMap() return mutable collections by contract.
practices.risk: If a method's result is meant to be a read-only view, failing to make that explicit lets callers mutate internal state unexpectedly.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Public getter-style methods returning Collectors.toList()/toSet()/toMap() results that represent a snapshot or internal view not meant to be mutated by callers.

practices.title: Returning Optional<List<T>>/Optional<Collection<T>> instead of an empty collection
practices.description: Wrapping a collection in Optional adds an unnecessary layer of null-handling ceremony on top of a type that already has a natural 'empty' representation, forcing every caller to unwrap before even checking for emptiness.
practices.risk: Every caller has to unwrap the Optional before it can even check whether the list is empty, adding ceremony a plain empty list would never have required.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Method signatures returning Optional<List<...>>, Optional<Set<...>>, Optional<Map<...>>, or any Optional-wrapped collection type.

practices.title: Obsolete object references in a manually-managed structure
practices.description: Effective Java Item 7: popping an element off a manually-managed array-backed stack (or removing from a cache) without nulling out the reference leaves the object reachable, so the garbage collector can never reclaim it.
practices.risk: A long-running service's memory grows slowly and steadily until it OOMs, and the leak is invisible in a short-lived test because it only shows up after enough push/pop cycles accumulate.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: manual array-backed collection whose remove/pop doesn't null out the vacated slot

practices.title: Ignoring ArrayList's capacity growth after a large temporary spike, causing lingering memory bloat
practices.description: ArrayList never shrinks its backing array automatically.
practices.risk: After a one-time large batch of additions followed by removals, the list keeps holding onto the larger backing array indefinitely unless trimToSize() is called, wasting memory for the remainder of the object's lifetime.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Long-lived ArrayList fields that experience large one-time growth spikes followed by clear()/removeAll(), with no trimToSize() call afterward.

practices.title: Magic numbers/strings instead of named constants
practices.description: A bare literal repeated across the codebase means the meaning lives only in the author's head, and every occurrence has to be found and updated together if it changes.
practices.risk: Six months later nobody remembers what the number means, or a typo'd literal in one of the many copies silently fails to match.

practices.title: Anonymous inner class where a lambda would be clearer
practices.description: Effective Java Item 42/43: for a functional interface, a lambda is shorter and avoids the anonymous class's confusing this (which refers to the anonymous class instance, not the enclosing object).
practices.risk: Code inside an anonymous class that calls this.someField silently reads the anonymous class's own field/method instead of the enclosing object's, a mistake a lambda's lexical this doesn't allow.
practices.solution: button.setOnClickListener(v -> handleClick());
practices.detectionPattern: new\s+\w+\s*\(\)\s*\{\s*@Override

practices.title: Overly broad variable scope
practices.description: Effective Java Item 57: declaring a variable well before its first use, or reusing a loop variable name across unrelated loops, makes it easy to accidentally reference a stale value from an earlier iteration or an unrelated code path.
practices.risk: Copy-pasting a loop body and forgetting to reset a variable declared outside both loops carries a stale value from the first loop into the second, silently.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: variable declared many lines before its first actual use

practices.title: Magic strings / stringly-typed code
practices.description: Using raw string literals as pseudo-enums (a status, a role, a mode) means a typo ("Admin" vs "ADMIN") compiles fine and fails silently at runtime instead of at compile time.
practices.risk: A typo'd literal in one of several scattered comparisons silently never matches, and the resulting bug looks like a logic error rather than the actual cause: a string that doesn't quite match.
practices.code:
if ("ACTIVE".equals(user.getStatus())) { }
map.put("role", "ADMIN");
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: the same string literal used repeatedly as a status/type/mode/role discriminator

practices.title: Deeply nested if-else / switch statements
practices.description: Nesting depth beyond 3-4 levels makes it hard to hold all the active conditions in your head while reading any single branch, and each new case multiplies the number of paths to reason about.
practices.risk: A bug fix added to the innermost branch doesn't account for a condition three levels up that the author lost track of while scrolling through the nesting.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: if/switch nesting depth greater than 3-4 levels

practices.title: Overly generic names (Manager, Handler, Processor, Util, data, info)
practices.description: A name like DataManager or process(Object data) reveals nothing about what the class or method actually does, forcing every reader to open the implementation just to find out.
practices.risk: Two unrelated pieces of logic both end up in a class called Utils or Manager because the vague name doesn't rule anything out, and the class slowly accumulates unrelated responsibilities.
practices.detectionPattern: class\s+\w*(Manager|Handler|Processor|Data|Info)\b

practices.title: Using size() == 0 instead of isEmpty() to check for an empty collection
practices.description: size() == 0 is functionally equivalent to isEmpty() for standard collections, but for some implementations (certain concurrent or linked structures) computing size() is O(n) or otherwise non-trivial, while isEmpty() is guaranteed O(1).
practices.risk: It also reads less clearly.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Conditional expressions of the form collection.size() == 0 or collection.size() > 0, which can be replaced with isEmpty()/!isEmpty().

practices.title: Manually counting frequencies with a HashMap instead of Collectors.groupingBy(..., counting())
practices.description: Hand-rolling a frequency count with getOrDefault()/merge() boilerplate is more verbose and error-prone than the standard Collectors.groupingBy(classifier, Collectors.counting()) idiom, which expresses the same intent in one line.
practices.risk: The hand-rolled getOrDefault() loop is more code to get wrong (an off-by-one, a missed increment) than the equivalent one-line Collectors.groupingBy(..., counting()) idiom.
practices.solution:
Map<String, Long> counts = words.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> w, Collectors.counting()));
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Manual loops building a frequency map with getOrDefault()/merge()/containsKey() where a stream over the same source is already used elsewhere.

practices.title: Multiple top-level classes in a single source file
practices.description: Effective Java Item 25: Java allows several top-level classes in one .java file, but which one 'wins' if the same class is accidentally defined in two files can depend on compilation order.
practices.risk: Two files each define a small unrelated Helper class at the top level; depending on compile order, the build silently picks one definition over the other with no error.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: more than one top-level class/interface declaration in a single .java file

practices.title: Using float/double for money or precise decimal calculations
practices.description: Binary floating-point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly, so arithmetic on float/double accumulates small rounding errors.
practices.risk: 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004; in a financial calculation these tiny errors compound across many operations into an amount that's visibly wrong at the cent level.
practices.solution:
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2"));
// use the String constructor, never `new BigDecimal(0.1)` (a double literal)
practices.detectionPattern: \b(float|double)\s+\w*(price|amount|total|balance|cost)\w*\s*=

practices.title: Relying on implicit narrowing conversions
practices.description: Assigning a wider primitive type into a narrower one without an explicit cast silently truncates or overflows the value instead of failing to compile.
practices.risk: A value of 130 assigned into a byte silently wraps around to -126 instead of raising any error, and the bug only surfaces much later when the wrong number is used downstream.
practices.code:
int value = 130;
byte b = (byte) value;  // silent overflow, no warning that data was lost
practices.detectionPattern: \bbyte\s+\w+\s*=\s*\(byte\)\s*\w+

practices.title: Preferring wrapper types over primitives in performance-sensitive code
practices.description: Boxing/unboxing a wrapper type (Integer, Long) on every loop iteration allocates an object where a primitive needs none, and introduces an unboxing NullPointerException risk that a primitive can't have.
practices.risk: A List<Integer> summed via a for-each loop silently throws an NPE the day one element happens to be null, in code that looks identical to summing a primitive array.
practices.solution:
int sum = list.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
// or filter nulls first if they're expected: list.stream().filter(Objects::nonNull)...
practices.detectionPattern: for\s*\(\s*Integer\s+\w+\s*:\s*\w+\)

practices.title: Using Boolean wrapper when a primitive boolean would do
practices.description: A Boolean field defaults to null (not false), which throws a NullPointerException the moment it's auto-unboxed into a primitive boolean context.
practices.risk: A newly-added Boolean field that's never explicitly initialized is null until set, and the first isActive() call on a fresh object throws an NPE instead of returning false.
practices.detectionPattern: private\s+Boolean\s+\w+;

practices.title: Missing input validation on a public method
practices.description: A public method that uses its parameters without checking them pushes the burden of correctness onto every caller, forever, instead of failing fast at the boundary.
practices.risk: A null or out-of-range value passed in from three call sites away isn't caught here; it propagates further into the system and fails with a confusing error far from where the bad value actually originated.
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: public method using its parameters with no null/range/blank checks

practices.title: Using System.out.println/e.printStackTrace() instead of a logger
practices.description: Console output has no log levels, no structured fields, and can't be routed, filtered, or aggregated the way a real logging framework's output can.
practices.risk: In production, this output either goes nowhere useful (no console attached) or floods stdout with no way to filter it by severity when investigating an incident.
practices.detectionPattern: \.printStackTrace\(\)|System\.out\.println\(

practices.title: Logging and rethrowing the same exception
practices.description: Logging an exception and then rethrowing it means the same stack trace gets logged again by whatever catches it further up, duplicating noise in the logs for a single failure.
practices.risk: An incident investigation finds the same error logged three times at three layers, making it unclear whether this was one failure or three separate ones.
practices.detectionPattern: log\.(error|warn)\([^)]*,\s*\w+\)\s*;\s*throw\s+\w+\s*;

practices.title: Incorrect log levels
practices.description: Logging routine, expected events at ERROR (or genuine failures at INFO/DEBUG) makes logs either too noisy to scan for real problems or hides the real problems entirely.
practices.risk: An on-call engineer's ERROR-level alert channel is full of routine page views, so a real production failure logged at the wrong level goes unnoticed alongside the noise.
practices.code:
log.error("User {} viewed page {}", userId, page);  // not an error
log.info("NullPointerException occurred", e);  // hides a real failure
practices.solution:
log.debug("User {} viewed page {}", userId, page);
log.error("Failed to process order", e);
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: business-as-usual event logged at ERROR, or an exception logged at INFO/DEBUG

practices.title: Not overriding toString() before logging collections of custom objects
practices.description: Logging a collection of objects that rely on the default Object.toString() prints unhelpful class-name-and-hashcode entries (e.g.
practices.risk: [com.example.Order@1b6d3586, ...]), giving on-call engineers nothing useful to debug with during an incident.
practices.code: log.info("Failed orders: {}", failedOrders); // prints [com.example.Order@1b6d3586, com.example.Order@4e25154f]
practices.detectionPattern: NO_CLEAN_REGEX: Custom domain classes stored in collections that are passed directly to a logger, without a meaningful toString() override.

practices.title: Ignoring the result of an immutable String method
practices.description: String is immutable — trim(), toUpperCase(), replace(), etc. all return a new String and leave the original unchanged. Calling one without using its return value does nothing.
practices.risk: Code that calls name.trim() expecting it to clean up name in place silently has no effect at all; the untrimmed value flows through unchanged.
practices.solution:
String name = "  Alice  ";
name = name.trim().toUpperCase();
practices.detectionPattern: \w+\.(trim|toUpperCase|toLowerCase|replace|strip)\([^)]*\)\s*;

practices.title: Misusing String.intern() on unbounded input
practices.description: intern() adds a string to the JVM's string pool, which lives for the life of the application. Interning strings derived from unbounded user input can grow that pool without limit.
practices.risk: Interning every distinct value of a high-cardinality user-supplied field (e.g. a search query) slowly grows memory that's never reclaimed, until the application runs out of heap.
practices.code: String s = userInput.intern();  // dangerous with unbounded/high-cardinality input
practices.solution:
// Avoid intern() outside a small, fixed, well-understood set of strings.
String s = userInput;
practices.detectionPattern: \w+\.intern\(\)

practices.title: Relying on the default platform charset
practices.description: String.getBytes() and new String(byte[]) without an explicit charset use the JVM's default platform charset, which differs across operating systems and JVM configurations.
practices.risk: Code that encodes/decodes text correctly in local development (UTF-8 by default) corrupts non-ASCII characters when it runs on a server or container with a different default charset.
practices.code:
byte[] bytes = str.getBytes();               // uses default charset
String s = new String(bytes);                // same problem
practices.solution:
byte[] bytes = str.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
String s = new String(bytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
practices.detectionPattern: \.getBytes\(\)|new\s+String\(\s*\w+\s*\)

practices.title: Using new String("literal")
practices.description: A string literal is already interned and shared. Wrapping it in `new String(...)` creates a redundant duplicate object and opts out of the string pool for no benefit.
